title: My son Absalom (2 Samuel 18:33)
hook: the rebellious son dies and David wishes he had died instead
carry: would god I had died for thee

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nathan's story of the little ewe lamb, and four words to a king. Your line was thou art the man. Where did the story turn out to be about you? Day four hundred six, the end of week fifty-eight.

Nathan warned David that trouble would rise from inside his own house, and it does. Years of it. A terrible wrong between his children, a revenge killing, a son sent into exile, then brought home but kept at arm's length. That son is Absalom: handsome, charming, famous for his thick hair. He sits by the city gate and listens to people's complaints, and tells them, if only I were judge, you'd get justice. Slowly he wins the hearts of Israel. Then he declares himself king, and David, old now, has to flee Jerusalem on foot, weeping as he climbs the Mount of Olives. Father and son are now at war.
screen: `TROUBLE FROM INSIDE THE HOUSE.` → `ABSALOM AT THE CITY GATE.` → `DAVID FLEES JERUSALEM, WEEPING.`

segments.voice: The armies meet in a forest. Before the battle, David gives his commanders one order, in front of everyone, and the Douay-Rheims puts it tenderly: "Save me the boy Absalom." The boy. A grown man leading a rebellion to take his father's throne, and David still calls him the boy. The battle goes against Absalom. Riding a mule under a great oak, his head catches in the branches, the mule runs on, and he's left hanging between heaven and earth. David's commander Joab finds him and, against the king's order, kills him. Then the messengers run to David, who is waiting between the city gates. The first is vague. The second says it plainly: may all the king's enemies be as that young man is. And David breaks. He climbs to the room above the gate, weeping, and says the words the whole story has been heading toward. The King James gives them like this: "O my son Absalom, my son, my son Absalom! would God I had died for thee, O Absalom, my son, my son!" Count how many times he says my son. He won the war and lost his child, and he'd trade the throne in a heartbeat. The Douay says it almost the same: would to God that I might die for thee. Christians have long heard something more in that cry: a father who would die in place of a rebellious son. David could only wish it. Christians believe that in Christ, God did it. And that's week fifty-eight: a shepherd chosen, a giant, a friend, a cave, a dance, a confession, and a father's grief.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for a broken family. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a family that's split. Maybe yours. Maybe a friend's. A parent and a child who don't speak, siblings who stopped coming to the same table, a divorce that left someone in the middle. Don't try to solve it. Just hold them, the way David held Absalom's name even in the middle of a war. If you pray, you can pray for them by name, and for whoever has stopped calling whom. If you don't, simply wish them peace. The bell holds the time.
My son Absalom. David's cry over the rebel son he still called the boy, wishing he had died in his place. Today's word.
Your line: would god I had died for thee. Today, reach toward one person in your family you've been holding at arm's length, even with one small word. Day four hundred six.

howItsDone: Catholics hear Absalom's rebellion and David's grief in the weekday Mass readings, and many pray for divided families at Mass, in the rosary, or by asking the intercession of Saint Monica, patron of parents with wayward children.

fork.setup: you're King David. your son has tried to take your throne and drove you from Jerusalem. your army is about to fight his. what do you tell your commanders?
fork.reveal: David orders them, in front of everyone, to spare his son. Joab kills him anyway, and the victory turns into grief.

original.note: Hebrew: my son. David repeats it again and again in his lament over Absalom.

trapdoor: what you thought: a rebellious son gets what he deserved.
what it means: David wins the war and loses his child, and would rather have died in his place. a father's love outlasts the betrayal.
what a scholar hears: Nathan warned that the sword would not depart from David's house; Absalom's death is the bitter end of that thread, and his cry repeats my son over and over.
